scientific_question: What structural features of the specified prochiral rotaxane can differentiate its two enantiotopic para sites in the first electrophilic amination, and what can substrate-level calculations establish about local site susceptibility and the limits of an enantioselectivity inference? This is an explanation task; the reaction observations are known context.

historical_record.rationale: The paper is in scope: it reports a small-molecule, homogeneous, CPA-catalyzed electrophilic aromatic amination/desymmetrization of a prochiral diarylamine-containing rotaxane in chloroform. The authors performed and reported non-routine DFT/NPA computations on the rotaxane substrate 1a in solution, including optimized conformers and a charge-distribution comparison of the two diarylamine aryl para positions. These computations address the reaction phenomenon of site/enantioselective desymmetrization. The public question is framed around the relative reactivity of the two enantiotopic aryl positions without exposing the authors' selected transition state, mechanism, or computed answer. The supplied evidence is sufficient to start a bounded computational study, although the exact Table S2 and full computational figure context should be retrieved for stronger verification.

DFT calculations were performed to study on the structure of prochiral rotaxane 1a in solution (toluene). Significantly, the non-covalent interactions observed in the X-ray structure of 1a (solid state) were all replicated in the calculated structure, including hydrogen bonding, parallel-displaced π-π interaction, and the \mathrm { C H } ^ { \cdots } \pi interactions between the macrocycle and axle subcomponents. Moreover, DFT calculations suggested that 1a existed as a pair of dynamic enantiomeric conformations, conformer 1a-A and 1a-B, wherein using ring A to attack the azodicarboxylate would facilitate the formation of the desired MPC rotaxane ( R _ { m p } ) _ { \mathbf { - } } 3 \mathbf { a }

conformer 1a-A The computational studies on the charge distribution of the rotaxane substrate 1a suggested that the para-position (C4-position) of the ring engaging in the parallel-displaced π-π interaction (ring A) with axle subcomponent is indeed relatively more electron rich (-0.277 a. u.) than the C4’-position of ring B without this interaction (-0.259 a. u.), which may render the mechanism involving TS-A more favorable.

Development of catalytic enantioselective synthesis of MPC rotaxanes through desymmetrization We began our study by selecting the prochiral rotaxane 1a with a diarylamine-containing macrocycle as the model substrate, which could be readily prepared using Leigh’s metal-free active template synthesis approach (Figure 2A).<sup>50,51</sup> We were delighted to find that the reaction of 1a with dibenzyl azodicarboxylate 2a (1.0 equiv) in the presence of various BINOL-derived CPA catalysts (10 mol%) at 25<sup>◦</sup>C in CHCl resulted in the anticipated desymmetrized rotaxane 3a with a varied er (see Table S1 in the SI for details), which was determined by chiral HPLC analysis in comparison with a racemic sample of 3a (Figure 2B). Among various BINOL-derived CPA catalysts examined, the CPA A1, featuring 3,3<sup>′</sup>-bis-(9-anthracenyl) groups, demonstrated the optimal enantioselectivity, which yielded the aminative desymmetrized MPC rotaxane 3a in 71% yield with 77.5:22.5 er. Transitioning from the BINOL-type to the SPINOL-type chiral scaffold using CPA A2 further enhanced enantioselectivity, resulting in the formation of 3a in 62% yield with 81:19 er. Furthermore, we were pleased to find that the incorporation of two bromine substitutions at the 10-position of the anthracenyl groups of the CPA catalyst (CPA (R)-A3) significantly improved the er value to 92:8. While further investigations into reaction solvents and temperatures did not improve enantioselectivity, we were thrilled to observe that increasing the quantity of 2a to 1.4 equiv resulted in the formation of MPC rotaxane 3a with 63% yield and 96.5:3.5 er. Encouragingly, a gram-scale reaction of 1a under the standard conditions produced product 3a (887 mg) in 67% yield with 96.5:3.5 er, demonstrating the practicability of this method for the synthesis of MPC rotaxanes. The utilization of the enantiomeric CPA catalyst ((S)-A3) in this reaction readily afforded the opposite enantiomer of the MPC rotaxane (ent-3a) in 62% yield with 3.5:96.5 er, whose enantiomeric relationship with 3a was clearly established through chiral HPLC analysis (Figure 2B). Moreover, a series of commercially available azodicarboxylates was examined with this method, all of which yielded the MPC rotaxanes 3b–3e with high to excellent enantioselectivities (up to >99.5:0.5 er) (Figure 2C).

D Sequential aminative desymmetrization and kinetic resolution decreased er value (75.5:24.5 er). This reduction in enantioselectivity may be attributed to the absence of π-π interaction between the macrocycle’s diphenylamine unit and the axle molecule’s bis(trifluoromethyl) benzene ring in the substrate, owing to an unfavorable spatial arrangement. Furthermore, a detailed analysis of the reaction progress over time under standard conditions revealed an initial enantioselectivity of approximately 90:10 er after 1 h, which then progressively increased to >95:5 er with the conversion of 3a into the di-amination product 5a (Figure 6B). This result suggested the potential kinetic resolution effect of the formation of the di-amination byproduct. As anticipated, treatment of racemic 3a with azodicarboxylate 2a (0.5 equiv) under the standard conditions resulted in the di-amination product 5a in 46% yield, with the recovery of 3a in 54% yield with 75.5:24.5 er, corresponding to a selectivity factor (s) of 6.6 (Figure 6C).<sup>53</sup> The recovered 3a was found to display the same configuration with the product accessed from the desymmetrization reaction. Moreover, the kinetic resolution of the racemic rotaxane 6a, bearing a Br-substituted dissymmetric macrocycle, was investigated with these conditions (using 0.7 equivalent of 2a), which yielded the MPC rotaxane 7a in 61% yield with 77.5:22.5 er and the recovered ent-6a in 36% yield with 94:6 er. Although the selectivity factor was not high ( s ~ = ~ 9 . 5 ) the recovered rotaxane could still be obtained with high enantioselectivity, emphasizing the practicability of this method for accessing MPC rotaxanes. Based on these results, a sequential desymmetrization and kinetic resolution mechanism was proposed for interpreting the high enantioselectivities of these reactions (Figure 6D). The enantioselective desymmetrization step favored the formation of enantiomer 3a, while the subsequent kinetic resolution step favored the rapid consumption of ent-3a, thus collectively enhancing the enantioselectivity of the MPC rotaxane product. Based on the control experiments and prior studies,<sup>48</sup> a plausible reaction mechanism was proposed (Figure 6E). Through the hydrogen bonding and π⋅⋅⋅π and C-H⋅⋅⋅π interactions between the axle amide and the macrocycle preorganizing the rotaxane conformation, the dual hydrogen bonding activation of both the diphenylamine N-H group and azodicarboxylate with the CPA catalyst creates a chiral environment, which facilitates the selective addition of aniline A’s para-position to the azodicarboxylate, likely due to its relatively higher electron density (see NPA charge analysis in Table S2 in SI for details). However, it is noteworthy that the mechanism involving the B-ring engaging in a parallel-displaced π-π interaction with the axle (the alternative dynamic enantiomeric conformer), while the less sterically hindered A-ring attacks the azodicarboxylate, is also a plausible scenario. This crucial step led to the formation of the desymmetrized dearomatized intermediate INT-A, which serves as the enantiodetermining step. Following this, the subsequent facile aromatization gave the para-CH-aminated (R )-rotaxane products 3.

historical_record.scientific_question: For the chiral phosphoric acid-catalyzed desymmetrizing electrophilic aromatic amination of the prochiral diarylamine-containing rotaxane substrate 1a with dibenzyl azodicarboxylate in chloroform at 25 °C, what controls the relative reactivity of the two enantiotopic diarylamine aryl positions during formation of the mechanically planar chiral rotaxane product?
historical_record.computation_relevance: The authors report DFT-optimized solution structures of rotaxane 1a and NPA charge analysis comparing the para-position of the aryl ring engaged in a parallel-displaced pi-pi interaction with the axle to the corresponding para-position of the other aryl ring. This directly supports a bounded investigation of relative aryl-site reactivity in the desymmetrizing amination reaction.

source_quotes.quote: Development of catalytic enantioselective synthesis of MPC rotaxanes through desymmetrization We began our study by selecting the prochiral rotaxane 1a with a diarylamine-containing macrocycle as the model substrate, which could be readily prepared using Leigh’s metal-free active template synthesis approach (Figure 2A).<sup>50,51</sup> We were delighted to find that the reaction of 1a with dibenzyl azodicarboxylate 2a (1.0 equiv) in the presence of various BINOL-derived CPA catalysts (10 mol%) at 25<sup>◦</sup>C in CHCl resulted in the anticipated desymmetrized rotaxane 3a with a varied er (see Table S1 in the SI for details), which was determined by chiral HPLC analysis in comparison with a racemic sample of 3a (Figure 2B). Among various BINOL-derived CPA catalysts examined, the CPA A1, featuring 3,3<sup>′</sup>-bis-(9-anthracenyl) groups, demonstrated the optimal enantioselectivity, which yielded the aminative desymmetrized MPC rotaxane 3a in 71% yield with 77.5:22.5 er. Transitioning from the BINOL-type to the SPINOL-type chiral scaffold using CPA A2 further enhanced enantioselectivity, resulting in the formation of 3a in 62% yield with 81:19 er. Furthermore, we were pleased to find that the incorporation of two bromine substitutions at the 10-position of the anthracenyl groups of the CPA catalyst (CPA (R)-A3) significantly improved the er value to 92:8. While further investigations into reaction solvents and temperatures did not improve enantioselectivity, we were thrilled to observe that increasing the quantity of 2a to 1.4 equiv resulted in the formation of MPC rotaxane 3a with 63% yield and 96.5:3.5 er. Encouragingly, a gram-scale reaction of 1a under the standard conditions produced product 3a (887 mg) in 67% yield with 96.5:3.5 er, demonstrating the practicability of this method for the synthesis of MPC rotaxanes. The utilization of the enantiomeric CPA catalyst ((S)-A3) in this reaction readily afforded the opposite enantiomer of the MPC rotaxane (ent-3a) in 62% yield with 3.5:96.5 er, whose enantiomeric relationship with 3a was clearly established through chiral HPLC analysis (Figure 2B). Moreover, a series of commercially available azodicarboxylates was examined with this method, all of which yielded the MPC rotaxanes 3b–3e with high to excellent enantioselectivities (up to >99.5:0.5 er) (Figure 2C).

The data of the X-ray crystallographic structures of 1a, 1l, 1o, and 12a have been deposited in the Cambridge Crystallographic Data Center under accession numbers CCDC: 2368661 (1a), 2368615 (1l), 2456077 (1o), and 2368663 (12a). These data can be obtained free of charge from the CCDC at https:// www.ccdc.cam.ac.uk/structures/. All other experimental, spectroscopic, crystallographic, and computational data are available in the supplemental information, including Tables S1–S7 and Figures S1–S20.

D Sequential aminative desymmetrization and kinetic resolution decreased er value (75.5:24.5 er). This reduction in enantioselectivity may be attributed to the absence of π-π interaction between the macrocycle’s diphenylamine unit and the axle molecule’s bis(trifluoromethyl) benzene ring in the substrate, owing to an unfavorable spatial arrangement. Furthermore, a detailed analysis of the reaction progress over time under standard conditions revealed an initial enantioselectivity of approximately 90:10 er after 1 h, which then progressively increased to >95:5 er with the conversion of 3a into the di-amination product 5a (Figure 6B). This result suggested the potential kinetic resolution effect of the formation of the di-amination byproduct. As anticipated, treatment of racemic 3a with azodicarboxylate 2a (0.5 equiv) under the standard conditions resulted in the di-amination product 5a in 46% yield, with the recovery of 3a in 54% yield with 75.5:24.5 er, corresponding to a selectivity factor (s) of 6.6 (Figure 6C).<sup>53</sup> The recovered 3a was found to display the same configuration with the product accessed from the desymmetrization reaction. Moreover, the kinetic resolution of the racemic rotaxane 6a, bearing a Br-substituted dissymmetric macrocycle, was investigated with these conditions (using 0.7 equivalent of 2a), which yielded the MPC rotaxane 7a in 61% yield with 77.5:22.5 er and the recovered ent-6a in 36% yield with 94:6 er. Although the selectivity factor was not high ( s ~ = ~ 9 . 5 ) the recovered rotaxane could still be obtained with high enantioselectivity, emphasizing the practicability of this method for accessing MPC rotaxanes. Based on these results, a sequential desymmetrization and kinetic resolution mechanism was proposed for interpreting the high enantioselectivities of these reactions (Figure 6D). The enantioselective desymmetrization step favored the formation of enantiomer 3a, while the subsequent kinetic resolution step favored the rapid consumption of ent-3a, thus collectively enhancing the enantioselectivity of the MPC rotaxane product. Based on the control experiments and prior studies,<sup>48</sup> a plausible reaction mechanism was proposed (Figure 6E). Through the hydrogen bonding and π⋅⋅⋅π and C-H⋅⋅⋅π interactions between the axle amide and the macrocycle preorganizing the rotaxane conformation, the dual hydrogen bonding activation of both the diphenylamine N-H group and azodicarboxylate with the CPA catalyst creates a chiral environment, which facilitates the selective addition of aniline A’s para-position to the azodicarboxylate, likely due to its relatively higher electron density (see NPA charge analysis in Table S2 in SI for details). However, it is noteworthy that the mechanism involving the B-ring engaging in a parallel-displaced π-π interaction with the axle (the alternative dynamic enantiomeric conformer), while the less sterically hindered A-ring attacks the azodicarboxylate, is also a plausible scenario. This crucial step led to the formation of the desymmetrized dearomatized intermediate INT-A, which serves as the enantiodetermining step. Following this, the subsequent facile aromatization gave the para-CH-aminated (R )-rotaxane products 3.

Public molecular inputs and scientific scope are unchanged.
historical_record.current_evidence_limits: Native evidence is one SMD-toluene local minimum and its mirror relation, not a CHCl3 ensemble or catalytic kinetic model. Final para NPA difference is −0.01241 e versus source −0.018 e; no hard numerical gate exists.
historical_reference_limitations: The supplied evidence gives only two numerical NPA charge values in a figure caption; the cited Table S2 is not included in the supplied evidence blocks.
The exact NPA charge-analysis protocol and any conformational sampling details are not fully available in the supplied evidence.
The computational result is a substrate charge-distribution and conformational analysis, not a full reaction-pathway or transition-state energy comparison.
The authors' computational solvation model is reported as SMD toluene, whereas the experimental reaction solvent is CHCl3; this limits direct quantitative comparison to experiment.
No uncertainty, error bars, or precision estimates are reported for the NPA charges.

current_scoring_authority.historical_record_role: All historical, source, numeric-tolerance and prior-acceptance records are non-scoring provenance. Do not restore their thresholds, intermediate inventories or review states. No historical acceptance classification is upgraded.
current_scoring_authority.evidence_requirement: Score only independent final scientific conclusions, totaling 100 points. Require actual executed calculations and recoverable native evidence for the molecular identities, composition, charge/spin, bonding, conditions, physical quantities and reference states relevant to each claim. Numerical energies, geometries and responses are evidence, never author-value targets or tolerance gates. A missing rounded scalar alone does not lose credit when the recoverable calculations establish the requested comparison. Do not restore numerical gates from historical references. Supplied observations, guessed conclusions, copied values, completed jobs, named intermediates and generic limitations earn no independent credit. Accept scientifically established equivalent explanations within the public scope without requiring author software, labels, a fixed intermediate inventory or an additional full reaction network. Method-sensitive alternatives must satisfy the specific criterion and actual evidence; a method change alone does not justify a contradictory claim. Return pass or fail for every item: a supported conclusion receives its whole weight, and an unsupported conclusion receives zero with a specific reason. Record demonstrated reference defects separately in objective_issue_flags; do not fabricate support or erase unrelated valid items. Infrastructure errors must be reported rather than disguised as scientific failures. Whole-case success requires every required_for_success item to pass, while independently supported items retain their points. Historical verification and structural package validation do not confer scientific acceptance.

historical_record_role: Pre-round-one evidence and qualification only; not additional current requirements or automatic acceptance.
